# Lecture 2: Probability foundations and random variables {#b02} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Lecture 2, you can - describe a random experiment with outcomes, events, and a sample space - combine events and compute probabilities from a table of counts - tell empirical proportions apart from model probabilities and forecasts - say what a random variable is and which values it can take ::: ::: {.driving-question} Driving question

Investors think in chances: how likely is a deal, how likely is a pitch from the show's later years, how likely are both at once. Before we can compute any such chance, we need a precise language for "how likely". This lecture introduces that language.

Pick one recorded pitch at random. What is the chance that it reached a deal, came from a late season, or both, and what do those numbers mean beyond this file? ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Do all the preparation below before class.
Video preparation
Watch Sample Space and Probability Axioms, then watch Definition of Random Variables. Be ready to define an outcome, sample space, event, and random variable. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide. The videos explain key ideas in another way and can use a different notation. The lecture material and its notation always come first.
[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Warm up.** In Lecture 1 you built frequency tables for the Shark Tank data. Build the season frequency table again. Once the data are loaded, you need one line of R: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) table(sharks$season) ``` ::: [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Predict.** Answer this question before you come to class. Pick one recorded pitch at random. Is the probability that the pitch reached a deal or comes from a late season larger or smaller than the probability of a deal plus the probability of a late season? Late means Seasons 9 to 16. Choose one answer. You find the answer in the lecture material. If set notation, complements, unions, or intersections are unfamiliar, review [Mathematics Refresher: sets and event notation](../resources/math-refresher.html#sets-and-event-notation). ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## Lecture material ### Start with a founder's question [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} You are preparing a pitch. Before you walk in, you would like answers to three questions. How likely is a deal at all? Was a deal easier to get in the later seasons, when the show was better known? How many pitches had both a late season and a deal? All three answers are in one small table. The code builds it from the Shark Tank file. "Late" means Seasons 9 to 16. The code first stores two yes-or-no answers for every pitch. `D` is `TRUE` when the pitch reached an on-air deal (`deal_on_show` equals 1). `L` is `TRUE` when the pitch comes from a late season (`season` is 9 or higher). Later in this lecture the same two letters name the two events. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 # TRUE if the pitch reached an on-air deal L <- sharks$season >= 9 # TRUE if the pitch is from a late season (9-16) table(deal = D, late = L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` late deal FALSE TRUE FALSE 330 229 TRUE 377 505 ``` ::: ::: The same counts with row and column totals: | | Early seasons (1--8) | Late seasons (9--16) | Total | |---|---:|---:|---:| | **No deal** | 330 | 229 | **559** | | **Deal** | 377 | 505 | **882** | | **Total** | **707** | **734** | **1441** | #### Answer by counting - **A deal at all.** 882 of the 1,441 pitches, 61.2%. - **A late season.** 734 of the 1,441 pitches, 50.9%. - **Both.** The bottom-right cell: 505 of 1,441, 35.0%. - **A deal, or a late season, or both.** Do not add 882 and 734. That would count the 505 pitches in the bottom-right cell twice. Count them once: 882 + 734 - 505 = 1,111 of 1,441, 77.1%. This answers the prediction from your preparation: the share is smaller than the sum of the two shares. - **No deal.** 1,441 - 882 = 559 pitches, 38.8%. One more comparison that a founder would want to see: among the late-season pitches, 505 of 734 got a deal (68.8%). Among the early ones, 377 of 707 did (53.3%). Lecture 4 is about comparisons of this kind. You have just used the main ideas of this lecture. The rest of the lecture gives these ideas names and symbols: outcomes and events, "and", "or", and "not", and the rules that say when you may add shares. With these names and symbols, you can use the ideas on any table and recognise them in any textbook. ### Why data analysis needs probability The shares above describe one fixed file. Most business questions are about a larger group, a population, but we see only a sample of it. A sample is one draw from the population, and another draw would give other numbers. Probability is the language for this uncertainty. [Lecture 7](b07-samples-estimators.qmd) shows this with the equity initially offered (`equity_offered_pct`) in the Shark Tank file. There the 1,441 records play the role of the population. One random sample of 100 records gives a mean that differs from the mean of all 1,441 records. Lectures 2 to 6 build the language of probability. Lectures 7 to 10 use it to go from a sample to a population. ### A probability model begins with possible outcomes

MIT explanation (review): 01.2 Sample Space.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Probability starts by describing exactly what may happen. A probability model needs a process, a list of complete possible results, and events that describe which results matter for the question. A **random experiment** is a process whose outcome is not known in advance. The word *random* does not mean "without any order or rule." It means that the model does not say in advance which possible outcome will occur. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Outcome, sample space, and event.** An **outcome**, written $\omega$, is one complete possible result of a random experiment. The **sample space**, written $\Omega$, is the set of all possible outcomes. An **event** is a set of outcomes, so it is a part of the sample space. An event occurs when the outcome that happens belongs to it. ::: The table shows how these terms fit together: | Object | Question it answers | Shark Tank example | |---|---|---| | experiment | What is done? | Select one of the 1,441 records at random, each with the same chance | | outcome $\omega$ | Which complete result occurred? | One complete selected pitch record | | sample space $\Omega$ | Which complete results were possible? | The set of all 1,441 records | | event $A$ | Which outcomes count as "yes" for this question? | The subset of records with an on-air deal | For a single roll of a fair six-sided die, $$\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.$$ The event $E=\{2,4,6\}$ means "an even result." The outcome $\omega=4$ belongs to $E$, so $E$ occurs when you roll a 4. The number 4 is an outcome. The set $\{4\}$, which contains only this one outcome, is an event. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check: is "the record with pitch_id 7" an outcome or an event? The record itself is one complete possible result of the selection, so it is an **outcome**. The description "the selected pitch is the record with pitch_id 7" describes the set that contains only that record, and a set of outcomes is an **event**. This is the same difference as the one between 4 and $\{4\}$ for the die. ::: #### An empirical selection experiment Define the experiment as **select one of the 1,441 recorded pitches uniformly at random**. The sample space is the set of 1,441 pitch records. Define two events: - $D$: the selected pitch reached an on-air deal - $L$: the selected pitch appeared in a late season (Seasons 9--16). These are the events behind the R objects `D` and `L` from the start of this lecture. Making the selection uniform means that every record has the same probability, $1/1441$. The probability of an event then equals its share of the records in this fixed dataset, so $D$ has probability $882/1441$. This does not mean that future entrepreneurs have the same probabilities. The box "What these numbers can and cannot say" below returns to this point. ### Combining events [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Events are sets of outcomes. So set notation gives us a precise way to describe how we combine events. | Notation | Name | Meaning | |---|---|---| | $A^c$ | complement | $A$ does not occur | | $A\cap B$ | intersection | both $A$ and $B$ occur | | $A\cup B$ | union | $A$, $B$, or both occur | | $A\subseteq B$ | subset | every outcome in $A$ is also in $B$ | | $\varnothing$ | empty event | the event that contains no outcome, so it never occurs | | $A\cap B=\varnothing$ | disjoint | $A$ and $B$ cannot occur together | As an example, suppose that we select one number at random from $$\Omega=\{1,2,\ldots,12\}.$$ Define $A=\{1,2,3,5,6,9\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3,4\}$. Each panel of @fig-b02-events shows the same sample space. A green circle means that the outcome belongs to the event named above the panel. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"} old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.6, 0.35, 2.8, 0.35), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i") omega <- 1:12 A <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9) B <- c(1, 2, 3, 4) event_sets <- list( setdiff(omega, A), intersect(A, B), union(A, B) ) panel_titles <- c("Complement", "Intersection", "Union") panel_meanings <- c("not A", "A and B", "A or B (or both)") draw_outcome_set <- function(selected, title, meaning) { plot(NA, xlim = c(0.45, 4.55), ylim = c(0.35, 4.2), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", asp = 1) title(main = title, line = 1.2, cex.main = 1.05, col.main = "#17324D") mtext(meaning, side = 3, line = 0.1, cex = 0.82, col = "#5B6976") rect(0.62, 0.55, 4.38, 3.55, col = "#F4F7F9", border = "#17324D", lwd = 1.4) text(4.18, 3.76, expression(Omega), cex = 0.85, col = "#17324D") x <- rep(1:4, 3) y <- rep(3:1, each = 4) is_selected <- omega %in% selected symbols(x, y, circles = rep(0.25, 12), inches = FALSE, bg = ifelse(is_selected, "#009E73", "white"), fg = ifelse(is_selected, "#009E73", "#9AA7B2"), lwd = 1.4, add = TRUE) text(x, y, labels = omega, col = ifelse(is_selected, "white", "#17324D"), font = 2, cex = 0.82) } for (i in seq_along(event_sets)) { draw_outcome_set(event_sets[[i]], panel_titles[i], panel_meanings[i]) } par(old_par) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Complement, intersection, and union of two events in a 12-outcome sample space. Green outcomes belong to the event named above each panel.](b02-probability-foundations_files/figure-html/fig-b02-events-1.png){#fig-b02-events width=768} ::: ::: So $A^c=\{4,7,8,10,11,12\}$, $A\cap B=\{1,2,3\}$, and $A\cup B=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,9\}$. Notice that "or" includes outcomes that are in both events: $1,2,3$ belong to the union as well as the intersection. The same notation works for business events. In the selection experiment, let $F$ be "the selected pitch is from the Food and Beverage industry" and $T$ "from the Technology/Software industry." Each record lists exactly one industry, so $F$ and $T$ are disjoint: $F\cap T=\varnothing$. The union $F\cup T$ is "a food or technology pitch," and $F^c$ contains every pitch from any other industry. Nothing new is needed. Only the sets have changed. Disjoint does not mean independent. If two disjoint events both have positive probability, observing one makes the other impossible. Independence, introduced in Lecture 4, means that observing one event does not change the probability of the other. #### The counts table again, with event names This is the table from the start of the lecture. The row and column labels now show the event names $D$ and $L$: | | Early ($L^c$, S1--8) | Late ($L$, S9--16) | Total | |--------------------|---------------------:|-------------------:|------:| | **No deal** ($D^c$) | 330 | 229 | **559** | | **Deal** ($D$) | 377 | 505 | **882** | | **Total** | **707** | **734** | **1441** | ::: {#exm-b02-events} ## Worked example: three events in words and symbols [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} From the table, describe each event in words and give its count. - $D^c$, "no on-air deal": the top row, $330 + 229 = 559$ records. - $D\cap L$, "deal and late season": the single bottom-right cell, 505 records. - $D\cup L$, "deal, late season, or both": every record except the top-left cell, $1441 - 330 = 1111$ records. This is the deal row (882) plus the late column (734) minus the 505 records counted in both. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Optional: more rules for combining events Four rules help to rewrite a combination of events. $A$, $B$, and $C$ are any three events. - First distributive law: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$. - Second distributive law: $A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)$. - First De Morgan rule: $(A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c$. "Not ($A$ or $B$)" is the same as "not $A$ and not $B$". - Second De Morgan rule: $(A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c$. "Not ($A$ and $B$)" is the same as "not $A$ or not $B$". In the counts table, $(D\cup L)^c=D^c\cap L^c$ is the top-left cell: the 330 early-season pitches without a deal. ::: ### Probability rules

MIT explanation (review): 01.4 Probability Axioms.

::: {.definition-box} Definition **Probability.** The probability of an event $A$, written $P(A)$, is a number between 0 and 1 that says how likely the event is. The closer the number is to 1, the more likely the event. An impossible event has probability 0, and a certain event has probability 1. ::: [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A model gives a probability $P(A)$ to each event $A$. These numbers must follow three rules: 1. **Non-negativity:** $P(A)\ge 0$ for every event $A$. 2. **Normalisation:** $P(\Omega)=1$. 3. **Additivity:** if $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, then $$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B).$$ The same holds for any finite number of events, as long as no two of them can occur together. The first two rules set the probability scale: probability cannot be negative, and something in the sample space must occur. The third says that you can add the probabilities of disjoint events, because no outcome is counted twice. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Optional: countable additivity In the formal theory the third rule also holds for infinite sequences of events, as long as no two of them can occur together, $P\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right) =\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} P(A_i)$. This matters for sample spaces with infinitely many outcomes. Every sample space in Lectures 2 to 5 is finite, so the finite version above is all you need there. ::: Write $|A|$ for the number of outcomes in the event $A$. For a finite sample space with equally likely outcomes, $$P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$ For example, $|D|=882$ and $|\Omega|=1441$, so $P(D)=882/1441\approx 0.612$. This ratio works only when all outcomes are equally likely. Here they are, because every record has the same chance of being drawn. #### Rules derived from the three above

MIT explanation (review): 01.5 Simple Properties of Probabilities.

Because $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint and together form $\Omega$, $$P(A^c)=1-P(A).$$ When $A$ and $B$ may overlap, $$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).$$ This is the addition rule. We subtract the intersection once, because it is counted in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. ::: {#exm-b02-union} ## Worked example: P(deal or late season), by hand [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Every number comes from the counts table above. Find each one in the table as you read. $$ P(D\cup L) =\frac{882}{1441}+\frac{734}{1441}-\frac{505}{1441} =\frac{882+734-505}{1441} =\frac{1111}{1441}\approx 0.771. $$ The 882 is the deal row total, the 734 is the late column total, and the 505 is the deal-and-late cell that both totals contain. We subtract it once, so that no record counts twice. This is the count from the start of the lecture, written as a rule: $P(D\cup L)$ is smaller than $P(D)+P(L)$ whenever the two events overlap, because the rule subtracts the overlap $P(D\cap L) > 0$. ::: Verification in R, with $D$ and $L$ built exactly as before: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( P_D = mean(D), P_L = mean(L), P_D_and_L = mean(D & L), P_not_D = mean(!D), P_D_or_L_direct = mean(D | L), P_D_or_L_rule = mean(D) + mean(L) - mean(D & L) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` P_D P_L P_D_and_L P_not_D P_D_or_L_direct 0.6120749 0.5093685 0.3504511 0.3879251 0.7709924 P_D_or_L_rule 0.7709924 ``` ::: ::: Three more properties follow from the three rules. You can see each one in the counts table. - The empty event has probability zero: $P(\varnothing)=0$. No record is both a deal and not a deal, so $D\cap D^c=\varnothing$ contains 0 of the 1,441 records. - A subset is never more likely: if $A\subseteq B$, then $P(A)\le P(B)$. The 505 late-season deals $D\cap L$ are part of the 882 deals $D$, and $505/1441\approx 0.350$ is below $882/1441\approx 0.612$. - An event can be split into two parts: $P(A)=P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap B^c)$. The 882 deals are the 505 late-season deals plus the 377 early-season deals, so $$P(D)=P(D\cap L)+P(D\cap L^c)=\frac{505}{1441}+\frac{377}{1441}=\frac{882}{1441}.$$ Lecture 4 uses this property again. ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Try it: P(no deal and early season) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Try this first with the student next to you. Complete the two missing steps before you open the answer. *Step 1 (given).* "No deal and early season" is the event $D^c\cap L^c$: the top-left cell of the counts table. *Step 2 (you).* Read the count for that cell from the table. *Step 3 (you).* Divide by the number of records and interpret the result in one sentence. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer $P(D^c\cap L^c) = 330/1441 \approx 0.229$: about 23% of the recorded pitches are early-season pitches that did not reach an on-air deal. Verification in R. The first two lines build `D` and `L` again: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 mean(!D & !L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2290076 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ### Partitions [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A **partition** divides $\Omega$ into events that do not overlap and together include every possible outcome. Each outcome belongs to exactly one part. For example, Seasons 1--8 and Seasons 9--16 partition the recorded pitches into an early-period event $L^c$ and a late-period event $L$ (@fig-b02-partition). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"} old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mar = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3)) plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i") rect(0.4, 0.4, 9.6, 4.6, border = "#17324D", lwd = 2) rect(0.4, 0.4, 4.9, 4.6, col = "#DCEAF3", border = NA) rect(4.9, 0.4, 9.6, 4.6, col = "#FDE5C1", border = NA) segments(4.9, 0.4, 4.9, 4.6, col = "#17324D", lwd = 2) rect(0.4, 0.4, 9.6, 4.6, border = "#17324D", lwd = 2) text(2.65, 2.5, expression(L^c), col = "#0072B2", cex = 1.25) text(7.25, 2.5, "L", col = "#D55E00", cex = 1.25) text(9.15, 4.15, expression(Omega), col = "#17324D") par(old_par) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The early-period event and the late-period event partition the sample space: no overlap, nothing left out.](b02-probability-foundations_files/figure-html/fig-b02-partition-1.png){#fig-b02-partition width=614.4} ::: ::: The two coloured regions do not overlap, and together they fill the whole rectangle. Lecture 4 uses this idea to combine probabilities from separate groups. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check: do the sixteen events "the pitch is from Season s" form a partition? Yes. Every record has exactly one season, so no two of the sixteen single-season events overlap, and together they cover all 1,441 records. $D$ and $L$, by contrast, do not form a partition: they overlap (505 records) and leave records out (the 330 early no-deal records). ::: ### From complete outcomes to numerical measurements

MIT explanation (review): 05.2 Definition of Random Variables.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} An outcome is a complete result, but an analysis usually focuses on one number that describes that result. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Random variable.** A number whose value depends on the outcome of a random experiment. A fixed rule turns each outcome into a number. ::: Random variables are written with capital letters, such as $X$. Their values are written with lower-case letters, such as $x$. Here are three random variables for our selection experiment: - the **deal indicator** $X$: equal to 1 when the selected pitch reached an on-air deal and 0 otherwise - the **season** $S$: the season number of the selected pitch - the **word count** $W$: the number of words in its written description. We fix the rule before we select an outcome. The value is unknown until then. That is the only sense in which the variable is "random." After the selection, the rule produces a number. This number, written in lower case as $x$, $s$, or $w$, is the **realised value** of the variable. A random variable is **discrete** when its possible values can be listed. A random variable is **continuous** when it can take every value in an interval, for example a waiting time. Lecture 6 treats continuous random variables. The **support** of a discrete random variable is the set of values it can take with positive probability. The support of the deal indicator is $\{0,1\}$. The support of season is $\{1,2,\ldots,16\}$. Lecture 3 gives a probability to every value in the support. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Optional: the formal definition of a random variable Formally, a random variable is a function from the sample space to the real numbers, $X:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$. Read left to right: $X$ takes an outcome $\omega$ from $\Omega$ and returns the number $X(\omega)$. For the deal indicator, $X(\omega)=1$ when $\omega\in D$ and $X(\omega)=0$ otherwise, so the event $D$ and the variable $X$ are linked by $D=\{\omega : X(\omega)=1\}$. The table lists the symbols: | Symbol | Meaning | |---|---| | $\omega$ | one complete outcome, such as one selected pitch record | | $X$ | the fixed measurement rule | | $X(\omega)$ | the number assigned by $X$ to outcome $\omega$ | | $x$ | a possible or realised numerical value of $X$ | ::: ::: {.caveat-box} What these numbers can and cannot say - $P(D)=882/1441\approx 0.612$ is exact for one question only: the chance of a deal when one record is drawn at random from this file. It is an **empirical proportion**. - It becomes a forecast for a future pitch only under four assumptions. The future pitch is like these pitches, producers select pitches in the same way, the process does not change over time, and "deal" keeps its meaning. - It says nothing about completed investments, which the file does not record. **What you can do with it:** use 61% as a first guess for a pitch on the show, and adjust it when you know more about the pitch. Lecture 4 shows how. ::: ### Answering the driving question Select one record uniformly at random. The chance that it reached a deal is $P(D)\approx 0.612$. The chance that it came from a late season is $P(L)\approx 0.509$. The chance of both is $P(D\cap L)\approx 0.350$, and the chance of at least one is $P(D\cup L)\approx 0.771$. Beyond this file, those numbers describe future pitches only under the four assumptions in the box "What these numbers can and cannot say". ::: {.founder-box} A founder's decision (invented example) Your order records show three shares among your customers: 12% had a late delivery, 8% gave a low rating, and 3% had both. You want to send a personal message to every customer with at least one of these problems. The addition rule gives the share: 12% + 8% - 3% = 17%. With 400 customers that is 68 messages, not the 80 that you would plan for if you simply added the two shares. The decision: 68 messages fit into one evening, so you send them this week. ::: **Next:** We can now give a probability to a single event, such as deal or no deal, late or early. Most business quantities have many possible values: which season, how many words, how many units sold. Lecture 3 moves from single events to the whole distribution of a random variable, which is a probability for every possible value. It also introduces two numbers that summarise a distribution: the expected value and the variance. ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class After the lecture, work through all the practice below. ### Read the lecture material Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the most important parts. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly. ### Recall questions 1. What is the difference between an outcome and an event? 2. What is the difference between a random variable and a realised value? 3. State the three probability rules. 4. Why is the ratio $|A|/|\Omega|$ for equally likely outcomes a special case? 5. What extra assumptions turn an empirical proportion into a forecast? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. An outcome is one possible complete result. An event is a set of outcomes that we define. 2. A random variable is a fixed measurement rule that turns outcomes into numbers. A realised value is the number produced for the observed outcome. 3. Probabilities are non-negative, $P(\Omega)=1$, and probabilities add across disjoint events. 4. The ratio $|A|/|\Omega|$ requires a finite sample space whose outcomes are equally likely. 5. A forecast needs a clearly defined target population. For a future pitch it also needs four assumptions: the future pitch is like these pitches, producers select pitches in the same way, the process does not change over time, and "deal" keeps its meaning. ::: ### Finish a half-worked example [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Re-read the worked union calculation (@exm-b02-union). Then complete the same calculation with new numbers: let $E=L^c$ be the early-period event (Seasons 1--8). *Step 1 (given).* From the counts table: $|D| = 882$, $|E| = 707$, $|D\cap E| = 377$. *Step 2 (you).* Apply the addition rule $$P(D\cup E)=P(D)+P(E)-P(D\cap E).$$ *Step 3 (you).* Interpret the result in one sentence. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer $P(D\cup E)=(882+707-377)/1441=1212/1441\approx 0.841$: about 84% of the recorded pitches reached an on-air deal, came from Seasons 1--8, or both. ::: ### Practice [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} In the uniform selection experiment, use $P(D)=882/1441$, $P(L)=734/1441$, and $P(D\cap L)=505/1441$. 1. Calculate and interpret $P(D^c)$. 2. Calculate and interpret $P(D^c\cup L^c)$. Hint: which records does this event leave out? 3. Are $D$ and $D^c$ disjoint? Explain. 4. Define a random variable $S$ that records the season of the selected pitch. State its support. 5. Define a deal indicator $X$. Explain how the event $D$ and the random variable $X$ are related but not the same object. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. $P(D^c)=1-882/1441=559/1441\approx0.388$: 38.8% of the records did not reach an on-air deal. 2. The event leaves out only the records that are both deals and from a late season, so $P(D^c\cup L^c)=1-P(D\cap L)=1-505/1441=936/1441\approx0.650$: 65.0% of the records did not reach an on-air deal, came from Seasons 1--8, or both. The addition rule gives the same result: $(559+707-330)/1441=936/1441$. 3. They are disjoint because a record cannot have and not have an on-air deal at the same time. 4. $S$ records the season number of the selected pitch record. Its support is $\{1,2,\ldots,16\}$. 5. $X$ equals 1 when the selected pitch is in $D$ and 0 otherwise. $D$ is a set of outcomes. $X$ is a measurement rule that assigns a number to every outcome. $D$ is the set of outcomes for which $X$ equals 1. ::: ### Review: one question from Lecture 1 A student concludes: "Our class survey had 180 responses, so its average risk score describes Dutch first-year students well. With that many responses, chance variation is small." Which problem does the size of the sample *not* solve? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Selection bias. A larger sample reduces sampling variability. But the class is a group from one programme that was easy to reach, not a random sample of Dutch first-year students. More responses from the same selected group do not make it more representative. ::: ### Worked exam interpretation [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Question.** R reports `mean(sharks$deal_on_show) = 0.612`. Is this an empirical proportion or a universal probability? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer It is first an empirical proportion: 882 of the 1,441 recorded pitches reached an on-air deal. It is also the probability of the event in a model that selects one of those 1,441 records uniformly. To use it for a future founder, you need four assumptions: the future pitch is like these pitches, producers select pitches in the same way, the process does not change over time, and "deal" keeps its meaning. ::: ### Check the AI [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} You asked an AI assistant: "How likely is it that a pitch got a deal or came from a late season?" It answered: > "P(deal or late) = 882/1441 + 734/1441 = 1616/1441 = 1.12. So the chance is about 112%." Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the **Verify** step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer A probability can never be above 1, so the answer must be wrong. The AI added the two shares and counted the 505 late-season deals twice. Subtract them once: (882 + 734 - 505)/1441 = 1111/1441, about 77%. A quick check for any probability: it must lie between 0 and 1. ::: ### Make it yours :::: {.utility-prompt} Two sentences about your own venture Think of your EiA venture, or any business you know well. Name one uncertain event that matters for it. Then write two sentences. First, define the event precisely (which outcomes count as "yes"?). Second, say how knowing its probability would change a real decision. There is no wrong answer. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run venture that sells boxes of prepared meals on campus.
